ECE 6390

Range differences and hyperbolas

From the figure to the concept

Fig. 1 shows three synchronized transmitters and a receiver: each pair’s range difference fixes one hyperbola branch, and two branches cross at the receiver.

A pseudorange is ρᵢ = Rᵢ + b + εᵢ, where Rᵢ is the geometric range, b is the receiver clock error expressed as a distance and εᵢ is measurement error, all in metres. The same b appears in every measurement taken at one epoch. Subtracting two measurements, Δρᵢⱼ = ρᵢ − ρⱼ = Rᵢ − Rⱼ + εᵢ − εⱼ, removes the clock term entirely.

All points with a fixed difference of distances to two foci form a hyperbola branch in a plane and a hyperboloid sheet in space. The sign selects the branch: a positive Rᵢ − Rⱼ places the receiver nearer transmitter j. A circle fixes the distance to one transmitter; a hyperbola fixes the difference between two.

Three transmitters give two independent differences in two dimensions, and their branches cross at the receiver. In three dimensions, four satellites give three differences. Once position is known, any one pseudorange recovers the clock offset b.

Differencing keeps the noise of both measurements. With independent errors of equal variance σ², Var(ε₁ − ε₂) = 2σ², and two differences that share measurement 1 have covariance σ². A tolerance on each difference widens its hyperbola into a band; where bands cross at a shallow angle the position is poorly determined, which is the geometry that dilution of precision measures.

Example

For transmitters at (−35, 0), (35, 0) and (0, 50) km and a receiver at (10, 15) km, the ranges are 47.43, 29.15 and 36.40 km. The differences are R₁ − R₂ = 18.28 km and R₁ − R₃ = 11.03 km, or 61.0 µs and 36.8 µs of arrival time. Adding a 12 km clock bias changes all three pseudoranges and neither difference.

Practice

1. Two transmitters are 70 km apart. Which measured range differences are physically possible?

The difference of distances to two points cannot exceed the distance between them.

Any difference with magnitude below 70 km. At ±70 km the branch collapses onto the line beyond one transmitter; a larger magnitude has no real position and signals a measurement error.

2. If each pseudorange has an independent error with σ = 3 m, what is the standard deviation of one difference?

Variances of independent errors add.

√(3² + 3²) = √18 ≈ 4.24 m. Differencing removes the shared clock but increases the random error by a factor of √2.
